summary:
**Nasutoceratops titusi** was a horned dinosaur that lived in what is now Utah about **76–75.5 million years ago**. Its fossils were found in the Kaiparowits Formation, and the species was formally named in 2013. Its name means “large-nosed horned face”; *titusi* honors paleontologist Alan L. Titus.

The best-known specimen is a nearly complete skull from a subadult, accompanied by some limb and other skeletal bones, plus rare skin impressions. The skull is about 1.5 metres long; the animal is estimated to have been around 4.5 metres long and weighed roughly 1.5 tonnes.

Its most striking features were a deep, short snout and exceptionally long brow horns. The horns curved outward and forward before turning inward and upward, reaching up to 457 millimetres—the longest known among centrosaurine ceratopsians. Its nasal horn was low and blade-like. The skull also had a nearly circular neck frill with low, crescent-shaped bony ornaments, including one at the top centre, unlike those of other known centrosaurines. Its nasal bones may have contained air-filled spaces, a feature not known in other ceratopsians.

Nasutoceratops was an early-branching member of **Centrosaurinae**, a group of horned dinosaurs, and may have belonged to its own subgroup, Nasutoceratopsini. The purposes of its horns and frill remain uncertain; proposed functions include display, species recognition, and combat. Its forward-pointing brow horns may have helped it lock horns with rivals, while its unusually deep snout may have been related to feeding.

It lived on **Laramidia**, the western landmass formed when the Western Interior Seaway divided North America. The Kaiparowits environment was rich in wetlands and supported a diverse dinosaur community. Nasutoceratops has also gained wider attention for its prominent nose and appearances in *Jurassic World* films.
